Regents of the University of California v. Bakke. In 1978, Allan Bakke, a white applicant, sued UC Davis Medical School after being rejected twice. He alleged he would have been admitted without the school's minority admissions program, which reserved sixteen of one hundred seats for minority students.

The Supreme Court voted 5 to 4, but the decision fractured. No single rationale commanded a majority. Justice Lewis Powell cast the deciding vote and wrote the plurality opinion. He held that schools may consider race as one factor among many in a holistic admissions process, matching the Harvard College model. However, Powell ruled that rigid numerical quotas violate the 14th Amendment's Equal Protection Clause. Bakke was ordered admitted.

For decades, universities used the decision to justify race-conscious admissions while avoiding formal quotas. They adopted holistic, individualized review processes that considered race among many factors, just as Powell had endorsed. The framework lasted forty years.

In 2023, the Supreme Court revisited the question in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard and restricted race-conscious admissions further, narrowing Bakke even more than it had already been narrowed. But for four decades after 1978, Bakke defined the law of affirmative action in American higher education, allowing universities to pursue diversity while respecting the constraint against rigid quotas.
